name: Eyelash implants
lead: Eyelash implants, also called eyelash transplantation, are surgical procedures in which hair follicles are placed along the eyelid margin to create, thicken or lengthen lashes. People seek them for a permanent fuller, darker lash line that frames the eyes without daily mascara, glued-on extensions or serums. They differ from temporary eyelash extensions or false lashes, which are applied to or alongside existing lashes.

The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia, often with mild sedation, with donor hair usually taken from the nape or the scalp behind the ears, though eyebrow or leg hair has also been used[3][4]. The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery describes candidates as people who lost lashes through trauma, burns, scarring, disease, cancer treatment or trichotillomania, as well as people with sparse lashes who want a cosmetic enhancement[3].

Ophthalmic plastic surgeons have raised concerns about cosmetic use. A 2007 EyeWorld report quoted Emory oculoplastic surgeon Anna Murchison saying cosmetic augmentation exposes the patient to unnecessary risks, and listed complications such as trichiasis, corneal abrasion and scarring[5]. Clinical literature is limited to case reports and a systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash transplantation[4][6].

A 2018 systematic review of 67 articles covering 354 patients from 18 countries, as summarised by a hair-transplant history article, reported generally positive outcomes with high satisfaction and improved lash density, along with a list of complications that includes infection, trichiasis and graft failure.[4]

paras: The surgeon makes tiny punctures in the lid margin and places individual hair grafts, spacing them to avoid trichiasis, where lashes grow inward. The procedure is done under local anaesthesia with optional mild sedation. A session takes one to three hours and the desired density usually takes one to three sessions.[3] The ISHRS notes that a normal upper lid has about 100 lashes and a lower lid about 60.[3]

Donor hair should match natural lash quality as closely as possible. Common donor sites are the nape of the neck and the scalp above or behind the ears; eyebrow and leg hair are also used.[3] The ISHRS says donor hair diameter and curl can make an aesthetic result look unattractive, and that people with congenital atrichia are candidates only for adhesive lash prostheses.[3] Preoperative preparation described by the society includes stopping anticoagulants such as aspirin and warfarin and vitamin E, avoiding alcohol and using an antiseptic facial soap.[3]

Itching is common for a day or more afterward; scratching can dislodge grafts, and some physicians recommend goggles at night or bandaging for the first 24 hours. Full recovery is described as taking 7 to 14 days.[3] Transplanted hairs typically shed within two weeks, with regrowth in four to five months.[4] Afterwards the lashes need lifelong care: lash oil, regular curling and regular trimming, because scalp hair keeps growing.[3][4]

Follicular unit-based transplantation is the most common approach, with temporal and occipital scalp the most frequent donor sites. Leg hair has been used for its finer texture and slower growth, and composite grafts from the eyebrow or sideburn have been used because they resemble lashes.[4] In a 2015 report of two patients compared leg hair and nape hair, both saw marked improvement in fullness within three months; leg-hair lashes needed trimming every five to six weeks versus every two to three weeks for nape hair, and did not need perming.[4] In a 2016 series of 15 patients with vitiligo-related lash whitening treated with follicular unit transplantation, 13 (86.67 percent) had a good to excellent response.[4]

The ISHRS says transplantation can give significant aesthetic improvement but cannot completely replicate natural lashes.[3] For people with unsatisfactory lashes, a 2022 report described a strip composite resection technique to remove transplanted lashes; in 10 patients (20 eyelids) the removed lashes did not regrow over one year of follow-up.[4]

The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery lists eyelid infection, bruising and swelling, graft displacement or failed growth, ingrown hairs, ectropion, entropion and poor graft placement or quality, such as from coarse donor hair.[3] A hair-transplant history article adds infectious folliculitis, blepharitis, graft asymmetry, recurrence of the original cause of lash loss such as scarring alopecia, and trichiasis that can risk corneal scarring.[4]

EyeWorld's 2007 report adds corneal abrasion and scarring, a foreign-body sensation and, in extreme cases, a threat to vision, and notes lashes that need ongoing trimming and may not look natural.[5] Ophthalmic plastic surgeons have also described a case of trichiasis after follicle transplantation (2007) and corneal punctate epitheliopathy secondary to trichiasis (2012).[4] The ISHRS cites a common US cost of $5,000 to $10,000.[3]

Eyelid surgery has a long record; the Code of Hammurabi is cited as evidence of eyelid surgery in ancient Babylon, though it is not known whether surgeons tried to restore lashes.[4] The earliest documented transplant attempt is Carl Heinrich Dzondi's in Halle in 1817 or 1818 using a fine pointed knife; Beck used an eyebrow-margin pedicle graft in 1838, Krusius a trephine and syringe in 1914 (up to 20 lashes per session, with about 50 needed for one eyelid), and Esser a flap technique in 1919.[4] Japanese work on hair grafting by Mutou and Boo-Chai (1962) fed the modern approach, followed by Beyer and Smith's 'Cilia transplant' in 1971 and Marritt's scalp-to-eyelash case in 1980.[4] A 2018 systematic review by Klingbeil and Fertig covered 354 patients, most of them women, with an average age of 29.[4][6]

Carl Heinrich Dzondi of Halle made the earliest documented attempt to transplant individual eyelashes in 1817 to 1818 [4]. Techniques using grafts of eyebrow margin (1838), a trephine and syringe (1914) and rotated lid-margin flaps (1919) followed, and Japanese dermatologists' work on small hair grafts fed the modern scalp-hair method in the late twentieth century [4]. A 2015 report described the first eyelash transplant using leg hair, and a 2016 series treated vitiligo-related lash whitening with follicular unit transplantation [4].

Separately, press accounts from 1882 and 1899 describe hair being sewn into eyelids to make false lashes [1]. Wikipedia recounts that false eyelashes were patented in the UK by Karl Nessler (filed 1902) and in the US by Anna Taylor (1911), and that in 1916 human-hair lashes fixed with spirit gum were used on actress Seena Owen in the film Intolerance [1]. Temporary lashes became popular in the early 1930s [1].

Prescription bimatoprost, sold for lashes as Latisse, is applied to the lash base to make small or underdeveloped lashes more prominent [2][7]. A registered study examined patient satisfaction with combined botulinum toxin, hyaluronic acid filler and Latisse for facial lines [8].

The ISHRS also mentions latanoprost, a glaucoma eye drop that lengthens and darkens existing lashes without stimulating new growth, noting eyelid inflammation, permanent iris darkening and temporary burning as side effects and advising caution for lash enhancement.[3]

A 2018 systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash hair transplantation covers the published case literature, with follicular unit techniques the most common and generally positive outcomes reported.[4][6] The published evidence is mostly case reports and small series; no controlled trials of cosmetic eyelash implants were found.

angle.text: Eyelash implants give a permanent fuller, darker lash line by placing hair grafts in the eyelid margin. The hairs are scalp or other body hair, so they keep growing and are trimmed and curled regularly.

card.summary: Surgical placement of hair into the eyelids for fuller lashes; only history is documented, with no outcome studies.
card.note: Surgery on the eyelid; no studies found.

quick.overview:
Eyelash implants are surgical procedures that put hair into the eyelid edge to build lashes. They are distinct from glued-on extensions.
Only historical mentions from the 1880s and 1890s exist.
quick.mechanism: Hair is placed into the lid margin so it grows as lashes.
quick.risks: Historical accounts describe the early method as painful. No modern safety or outcome studies were found.
